AND org_id = ? projecting only required columns; - Two-step: SELECT by id then check org_id in app logic; - DB-enforced tenancy: Row-Level Security (RLS) or equivalent DB policy with SELECT by id only; 4) Trade-offs: single-SELECT is simplest, lowest latency, clear 404 semantics, easy to test and maintain; two-step is slightly more complex and risks accidental existence leakage if not carefully coded; RLS gives strongest enforcement at the DB layer and future-proofs tenancy but adds DB policy complexity and operational overhead; 5) Recommendation: implement the single parameterized SELECT that includes org_id from the JWT, validate workflow_item_id shape (e.g. UUID) before querying, return 404 when no row, use prepared statements/ORM parameterization to avoid injection, project only required columns, add unit/integration tests and minimal audit logging; 6) Follow-ups/validations needed: confirm workflow_item_id datatype and DB column names, decide whether assignee should be id vs display name and whether to join users table, confirm JSON field naming/time format (RFC3339), and agree logging/audit level and whether/when to migrate to DB RLS for stronger enforcement.

rounds.response: 1) Restate the decision: implement a tenant-safe GET /workflow_items/{workflow_item_id} in the existing Nimbus backend that returns JSON {id, title, status, assignee, last_updated_at (RFC3339 UTC)}; soft-deleted rows (deleted_at != NULL) must be treated as not-found and the endpoint must return 404 for any well-formed-but-missing or cross-tenant item, 400 for malformed IDs, and 500 for internal errors. 2) Assumptions & constraints: low traffic, use existing primary relational DB and current REST/JWT conventions (JWT contains org_id and user_id), use existing ORM and error format, soft-delete via deleted_at, scope strictly limited to this single lookup, and do not leak existence across tenants. 3) Key options: - Single-SELECT with WHERE id = ? AND org_id = ? AND deleted_at IS NULL projecting only required columns; - Two-step read-then-check where app logic enforces org_id/deleted_at; - DB-level enforcement (RLS or a tenant-filtering view) that centralizes tenancy/deleted_at policy. 4) Trade-offs: Single-SELECT is simplest, minimal latency, aligns with current patterns and yields straightforward 404 semantics; Two-step is more error-prone and easier to accidentally log/leak existence; DB-level enforcement is most robust for long-term multi-tenant safety but adds DB policy complexity and operational overhead that’s unnecessary for this small feature. 5) Recommendation and implementation notes: implement the Single-SELECT via ORM/prepared statement: SELECT id, title, status, assignee, updated_at FROM workflow_items WHERE id = :id AND org_id = :org_id AND deleted_at IS NULL; validate workflow_item_id syntactically (UUID) and return 400 if malformed, convert updated_at to RFC3339 UTC as last_updated_at, return 404 if no row, use parameterized queries to avoid injection, add unit/integration tests covering malformed ID/other-org/soft-deleted/success cases, and include minimal audit logging (tenant org_id, actor user_id, request_id, outcome, timestamp) while avoiding leaked existence: log the full workflow_item_id only on 200 success, and for 404s log a non-reversible HMAC(id) or masked id plus the org_id and outcome to enable correlation without making probing easy. 6) Follow-ups/validations needed before implementation: confirm JWT claim names for org_id/user_id, confirm workflow_items column names and that assignee should be id vs display name (and whether a join to users is allowed), confirm exact RFC3339 formatting expectations, agree on HMAC key management and log retention/permissions, and decide if/when to migrate to DB RLS for stronger enforcement.

However, the Security Officer calls out that the HMAC/logging strategy and error handling will need to be consistently applied to any future lookup endpoints, and the Engineering Lead asks for a small extension to the response shape to avoid another near-term change.
